content: Wilson's disease, first identified by Samuel Wilson in 1912, is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene. This condition arises due to the accumulation of copper in various tissues. Diagnosing Wilson's disease is challenging because there is no definitive gold standard test, and the clinical presentation is often non-specific. Diagnosis typically requires a combination of clinical evaluation and laboratory tests, which can lead to delays in diagnosis. Such delays may negatively impact patient outcomes and have implications for the timely diagnosis of other family members. The Leipzig criteria, established in 2003, were designed to standardize the diagnosis and management of Wilson's disease. However, these criteria have not been formally validated, and this review focuses on the evidence supporting the use of biochemical tests for diagnosing Wilson's disease. The objective of this review was to assess the diagnostic accuracy of three specific biochemical tests—caeruloplasmin levels, 24-hour urinary copper excretion, and hepatic copper content—at defined cut-off values for diagnosing Wilson's disease. These tests were evaluated in individuals suspected of having Wilson's disease and compared to appropriate control groups, which included healthy individuals or those with chronic liver diseases unrelated to Wilson's disease. Since there is no definitive gold standard for diagnosing Wilson's disease, the Leipzig criteria were used as the clinical reference standard. The review also aimed to determine whether these tests should be universally applied to all individuals recommended for Wilson's disease testing or restricted to specific subgroups. The studies included in this review were identified through extensive searches of databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), PubMed, Embase, the Web of Science, and clinical trial registries, with the most recent search conducted on May 29, 2019. Both prospective and retrospective cohort studies that evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of the index tests using the Leipzig criteria as the reference standard were included. Two independent reviewers assessed the methodological quality of the studies using the QUADAS-2 tool. Although meta-analyses were planned to evaluate the sensitivity and specificity of each biochemical test, differences in methodologies across studies precluded this, and the results were instead described narratively. Eight studies, involving a total of 5,699 participants (1,009 of whom were diagnosed with Wilson's disease), met the inclusion criteria. Three studies focused exclusively on children, one on adults, and the remaining four included both children and adults. Two studies evaluated participants with hepatic symptoms, while six included individuals with a combination of hepatic and neurological symptoms, as well as pre-symptomatic individuals. The methodological quality of the studies varied, with significant concerns about participant selection and the reference standards used. Differences in assay methods, diagnostic thresholds, and the demographic characteristics of study populations (e.g., age and ethnicity) further complicated the interpretation of results. These methodological concerns suggest that the diagnostic accuracy reported in these studies may not be generalizable to other populations. Caeruloplasmin as an index test: Five studies, involving 4,281 participants (541 with Wilson's disease), evaluated various thresholds for caeruloplasmin levels. Using a cut-off of 0.2 g/L, as recommended by the Leipzig criteria, the sensitivity ranged from 77.1% to 99%, while specificity varied between 55.9% and 82.8%. Lowering the cut-off to 0.1 g/L reduced sensitivity to 65%–78.9% but increased specificity to 96.6%–100%. Hepatic copper as an index test: Four studies, involving 1,150 participants (367 with Wilson's disease), assessed hepatic copper content. A cut-off of 4 μmol/g, as specified in the Leipzig criteria, yielded a sensitivity of 65.7%–94.4% and a specificity ranging from 52.2% to 98.6%. 24-hour urinary copper as an index test: Three studies, involving 268 participants (101 with Wilson's disease), evaluated 24-hour urinary copper excretion. Using a cut-off range of 0.64–1.6 μmol/24 hours, as per the Leipzig criteria, sensitivity varied from 50.0% to 80.0%, while specificity ranged from 75.6% to 98.3%. The authors concluded that the diagnostic thresholds for caeruloplasmin, 24-hour urinary copper, and hepatic copper are highly dependent on the methods used and require validation in the specific populations where these tests will be applied. The evidence does not support the use of binary cut-offs or single-test strategies to definitively rule in or rule out Wilson's disease. Additionally, there is insufficient evidence to guide testing in specific subgroups defined by age, ethnicity, or clinical presentation.
